issue: Identifying columns are encrypted at rest, so a created object cannot be matched by plaintext name in the business tables (sso_lobs.sls_name, sso_users.ssu_username, sso_services.ss_username / ss_server_ip / ss_server_host).
recommended_solution: Validate through sso_arcos_log, whose sal_object_referance holds the PLAINTEXT object name, filtered by aot_description (object type), aoo_object_operation ('Created'/'Modified'/'Deleted') and sal_Api_user_id IS NOT NULL, then confirm durability with a scoped COUNT on the business table using created_by='SYSTEM_API' plus a timestamp window.
recommended_advantages: Needs no encryption key and no product crypto code. Survives a future fix to the deterministic-encryption weakness. Covers create, update and delete in one channel, and sal_old_value/sal_new_value give real update assertions. Verified working: 5 run-attributable rows retrieved including 2 creates and 1 delete.
recommended_disadvantages: The audit log over-reports creates 6:1 (DB-006), so it must always be paired with a business-table check. aot_description values are only known for 'User Transactions' and 'Service Transactions' - the rest must be catalogued first. Two queries per assertion instead of one.
recommended_effort: M - roughly 3-5 days: catalogue aot_description per object type, add two DBUtils methods, wire into the create/update/delete assertions.
alternative_solution: Ciphertext-equality lookup: read the ciphertext back once from the row the API created, keep it as a fixture, and match on it thereafter (WHERE ssu_username = '<ciphertext>'). Works because encryption is deterministic.
alternative_advantages: Single query, hits the authoritative business table directly, no dependency on audit-log semantics. Verified: the lookup returned exactly 1 row for the run-created user.
alternative_disadvantages: Cannot construct the ciphertext for a NEW name without the key, so it only validates 'the row I created still exists', not arbitrary lookups. Breaks completely the day the product adds a per-row IV - which is the recommended security fix in SOL-DB-003. Couples test fixtures to ciphertext blobs that are unreadable in code review.
evidence_ref: DB-003, DB-004, DB-005, DB-006; db-schema-map.json validation_levers.lever_1_audit_log_plaintext and lever_2_ciphertext_equality

issue: The validation account is sysadmin. Environments/QA_MsSQL.properties points db_user at 'devops', which holds sysadmin and dbcreator with 34 server-level permissions over 31 databases, and the password is committed in plaintext.
recommended_solution: Provision a dedicated least-privilege login (e.g. pam_qa_validator): CONNECT to ARCOSDB_U16SP2_WEBSM_QA only, SELECT granted on an explicit table whitelist, no server roles, no db_datareader, and explicit DENY on sso_ApiUsers and tbl_KeyEncryptionDecryption. Point db_user at it and add a DBUtils startup guard that aborts if IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin') = 1.
recommended_advantages: Removes all destructive authority, so no generated or mistyped statement can damage 31 databases. The DENY pair keeps cleartext credentials and private key material out of test reach. The startup guard makes the control self-enforcing rather than documentary. Whitelist grants also document exactly which tables validation depends on.
recommended_disadvantages: Needs a DBA to create the login and grants, so it is externally blocked. The whitelist must be extended whenever a new object is validated, which is friction. Existing plaintext credential still needs rotating and purging from git history.
recommended_effort: S for the framework side (1 day: guard plus config), but blocked on a DBA request - allow a week of lead time.
alternative_solution: Keep the devops login but force read-only at the connection level: ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly in the JDBC URL, connection.setReadOnly(true), and a statement-level allowlist in DBUtils that refuses any SQL not beginning with SELECT or WITH.
alternative_advantages: Implementable immediately with no DBA dependency. The statement allowlist is the same control already proven in tools/obj007_db_probe.ps1, which refused everything except SELECT/WITH throughout this investigation.
alternative_disadvantages: Defence in the client only - the credential still holds sysadmin, so anything that bypasses DBUtils (a debug session, a stray script, a leaked properties file) has full destructive authority. setReadOnly is advisory for SQL Server and does not actually block writes. Leaves a sysadmin password in version control.
owner_team: DBA / Infrastructure, with QA Automation for the framework guard

issue: Column encryption is deterministic with a static key and no per-row IV, functionally equivalent to AES-ECB. 91% of services share one ss_port ciphertext, and one ciphertext appears in three columns across two tables, so plaintext distribution leaks to anyone with read access.
recommended_solution: Move to randomised encryption with a per-row IV, or adopt SQL Server Always Encrypted with randomised encryption type for the identifying columns, with keys held in the existing HSM path (sso_hsm_config indicates HSM support already exists).
recommended_advantages: Eliminates frequency analysis - identical plaintext no longer yields identical ciphertext. Always Encrypted keeps keys out of the database entirely, which also fixes SOL-DB-004. Aligns the product with standard practice for credential-bearing columns.
recommended_disadvantages: Breaks every equality lookup the application currently performs on those columns, so it is a substantial product change with a data migration for 20,651 services and 1,439 users. Randomised Always Encrypted forbids server-side equality predicates, which the application likely relies on. Will also break the ciphertext-equality test lever, so SOL-DB-001's recommended (audit-log) path must land first.
recommended_effort: L - a product-team programme, multiple sprints including migration and regression.
alternative_solution: Keep deterministic encryption but scope the key per column and add a per-column salt, so at minimum a ciphertext cannot be correlated across columns and tables.
alternative_advantages: Much smaller change; equality lookups keep working, so the application needs little rework. Removes the cross-table correlation that is the most immediately exploitable part of the weakness.
alternative_disadvantages: Does not fix the core problem - within a single column, frequency analysis still recovers common values such as the default port shared by 18,848 rows. A partial mitigation presented as a fix risks closing the finding prematurely.
alternative_effort: M - one product sprint plus migration.

issue: Secrets are stored in cleartext in the database: sso_ApiUsers holds Password, UsersSecret and UsersKey in plaintext for 34 API users, and tbl_KeyEncryptionDecryption holds unencrypted private key material in the same database as the data it protects.
recommended_solution: Salted-hash the API user password (it is only ever verified, never replayed), move UsersSecret / UsersKey and the keypair into a secret store or the existing HSM, and revoke SELECT on both tables from every account that does not strictly need it.
recommended_advantages: Removes the single highest-value target in the schema. Read access to the database would no longer yield working API credentials or the key that protects every encrypted column, which currently makes the encryption in SOL-DB-003 moot. Hashing a verify-only password is a well-understood, low-risk change.
recommended_disadvantages: Requires product changes in the API authentication path plus a migration for 34 users, and any integration that reads the password back from the database will break - which has to be discovered first. HSM integration adds an operational dependency.
recommended_effort: M-L - one to two product sprints, plus an audit for consumers that read these columns.
alternative_solution: Interim containment: leave storage as-is but revoke SELECT on sso_ApiUsers and tbl_KeyEncryptionDecryption from all non-application principals, rotate the 34 exposed credentials and the keypair, and add a DENY for the test account.
alternative_advantages: Deployable immediately with no code change, and it shrinks the blast radius while the real fix is scheduled. Rotation invalidates anything already harvested.
alternative_disadvantages: The secrets remain in cleartext, so any account with sufficient rights - including the devops sysadmin login currently in QA_MsSQL.properties - still reads them. Backups, replicas and DBA access remain exposed. Containment only, not a fix.
owner_team: Product Engineering (PAM core) with DBA for the interim grants

issue: The database declares only 5 foreign keys across 552 tables, so referential integrity is enforced only in application code. 16,560 of 313,197 ssR_Users_Services rows (5.3%) point at services that no longer exist, plus 9 orphaned lobs_users rows, 17 users with no detail row, and 5 drifted denormalized LOB names.
recommended_solution: Add the four measured orphan queries and the denormalization-drift query to the framework as standing integrity assertions, baseline the current counts, and raise the 16,560 orphans to the product team as a delete-path defect.
recommended_advantages: Needs no encryption handling at all - pure ID joins. Finds real defects immediately rather than guarding a hypothetical. Orphaned user-to-service authorisation rows are security-relevant in a privileged-access product, so the finding carries weight. Baselining means CI fails only on new orphans.
recommended_disadvantages: The joins scan large tables (313,197 rows for the biggest), so they belong in a nightly job rather than per-test. Baselining risks normalising 16,560 existing defects if the baseline is never revisited - it needs an explicit burn-down owner.
recommended_effort: S - 2-3 days for the assertions and baseline; the product-side cleanup is separate.
alternative_solution: Ask the product team to declare the missing foreign keys so the database enforces integrity itself.
alternative_advantages: Fixes the cause rather than detecting the symptom, and prevents new orphans at write time rather than reporting them later. No test code needed.
alternative_disadvantages: Cannot be applied until the 16,560 existing orphans are cleaned, since the constraints would fail to create. High regression risk - the application may depend on writing rows in an order that FKs forbid, or on soft-delete behaviour that hard FKs break. Realistically a long programme, and it does not address the denormalization drift at all.
alternative_effort: L - product programme, gated on data cleanup.
owner_team: Product Engineering (PAM core) for the cause; QA Automation for the assertions

issue: The audit log over-reports creation - 6 rows claim 'Created / User Transactions / AUTO40PC47' while only 1 sso_users row and 1 sso_ApiUsers row exist. It records the attempt, not the durable insert, mirroring the API's Success:true / Message:'Already Exists' trap.
recommended_solution: Make every create assertion two-part and report the parts separately: (1) the audit log has a matching 'Created' row for the plaintext reference within the run window, and (2) a scoped business-table COUNT confirms the row is durably present. Fail if either part fails, and surface a divergence between them explicitly.
recommended_advantages: Neither channel can produce a false pass alone, and reporting them separately makes the 6-versus-1 divergence visible instead of averaging it away - that divergence is itself the product defect. Directly closes the same class of gap as the Already-Exists trap.
recommended_disadvantages: Two queries per create assertion, and the reporting model must carry two sub-verdicts rather than one boolean, which means touching the Excel report writer as well as DBUtils.
recommended_effort: M - 3-5 days including the report-shape change.
alternative_solution: Assert only on the business table, using created_by='SYSTEM_API' plus a timestamp window, and ignore the audit log for creates.
alternative_advantages: Simplest possible check, one query, and the business table is authoritative on durability - it cannot over-report.
alternative_disadvantages: Loses the plaintext name match, so for encrypted objects the assertion degrades to 'some row was created by the API in this window', which under the concurrent activity documented in DB-022 is weak. Also discards the audit log's old/new values, which are the only sound basis for update assertions.

issue: A background provisioning job is permanently broken, emitting a flat 240 errors per hour indefinitely (about 2.1M rows a year). It inflated the run-window error count from 194 genuinely test-attributable rows to 1,736, and the TargetDeviceOnboarding callback path is non-functional in QA.
recommended_solution: Raise as a product defect against TargetDeviceOnboardingController.CallBack (APA:DOC0010) and DatabaseCRUD.UpdateTargetUserCreationStatus (APA:DL0046) - an empty result set is indexed at position 0 without a guard, throwing IndexOutOfRangeException. Separately, require every DB-based error analysis to filter by IpAddress or ApplicationName before attributing errors to a test.
recommended_advantages: Fixes a real broken feature and stops 2.1M log rows a year. Removes an 8:1 noise ratio that would otherwise make any error-log-based assertion unusable. The failing pair and the exception are precisely identified, so the defect report is actionable.
recommended_disadvantages: Depends on the product team's queue - the framework cannot fix it. Until it lands, every error-log assertion carries a filter that must be maintained.
recommended_effort: S for the defect report and the framework filter (1 day); product fix effort is theirs to size.
alternative_solution: Treat it purely as test-side noise: baseline the known-broken methods in an exclusion list and subtract them from error counts, without pursuing the product fix.
alternative_advantages: Immediate, entirely within QA's control, and unblocks error-log assertions today.
alternative_disadvantages: Leaves a broken product feature unreported, which is a QA failure in itself. The exclusion list silently hides a whole code path, so a genuine new failure in CallBack would never be noticed. Log growth continues.
owner_team: Product Engineering (Provisioning) for the fix; QA Automation for the filter

issue: ArconPamApiLog holds 41,910,875 rows with only a clustered PK on LogId. LoggedOnDate, ApplicationName, Level and Method are unindexed, so any date or application filter is a full 41.9M-row scan on a live application database. Six years of logs are retained with no purge.
recommended_solution: In the framework, never filter this table by date alone - binary-search LogId to the target timestamp using the clustered index (SELECT TOP 1 LogId, LoggedOnDate FROM ArconPamApiLog WHERE LogId >= N ORDER BY LogId), then bound the real query by a LogId range. Encode this as the only available access path in DBUtils. Recommend a nonclustered index on (ApplicationName, LoggedOnDate) and a retention policy to the product team.
recommended_advantages: Works today with no schema change and no DBA involvement, on a table the test account only reads. Proven throughout this investigation - every ArconPamApiLog query here used it and returned in seconds instead of minutes. Encoding it in DBUtils stops a future author reintroducing the scan.
recommended_disadvantages: More complex client-side logic than a plain WHERE clause, and it assumes LogId order tracks LoggedOnDate order - true for an identity column with sequential inserts, but it is an assumption, not a constraint. Does nothing about the underlying index gap or the unbounded growth.
recommended_effort: S - 1-2 days for the helper plus the recommendation write-up.
alternative_solution: Request the nonclustered index on (LoggedOnDate) and (ApplicationName, LoggedOnDate) and then query the table normally by date.
alternative_advantages: Removes the problem at source; every consumer benefits, including support engineers, not just the test framework. Query code stays simple and obvious.
alternative_disadvantages: Needs DBA approval and a maintenance window - adding an index to a 41.9M-row table on a live system is not free, and it increases write cost on the hottest logging path in the product. Does not address retention.
owner_team: DBA / Product Engineering; QA Automation for the client-side helper

issue: ApiHelper's KNOWN_ERROR_CODES = {201, 202, 203} bears almost no relation to the codes the product actually emits. The database shows structured family-controller-method codes such as '903- SDC-SFS', '902-UDC-ULN', '902SPB-GSP', 'APA:DL0046', 'APA:Decrypt0001', and a single endpoint can emit several distinct codes.
recommended_solution: Harvest the real catalogue from the database rather than maintaining a hand-written set: SELECT DISTINCT Message FROM ArconPamApiLog WHERE ApplicationName='ARCONPAMAPI' AND Level='ERROR', bounded by a LogId range, and load the result as framework data.
recommended_advantages: Replaces guesswork with measurement, and the codes are structured rather than numeric so a numeric-only set can never match them. Self-maintaining - a re-harvest picks up new codes. The same query also feeds the error-log assertion in SOL-DB-007.
recommended_disadvantages: Only captures codes that have actually occurred in the retained log window, so it is a lower bound, not the definitive catalogue. Requires the LogId-bounding discipline from SOL-DB-008. Codes appear as free-text log messages, so parsing needs care and will need cleanup rules.
recommended_effort: S - 2 days to harvest, parse and load.
alternative_solution: Request the authoritative error-code catalogue from the product team or extract it from the product source, and replace the hardcoded set with that.
alternative_advantages: Complete and authoritative rather than observation-limited, including codes no test has yet triggered, and it carries the intended meaning of each code - which the log messages do not.
alternative_disadvantages: Depends on documentation that may not exist or be current - the owner has already confirmed the API reference is out of date, and only 4 error codes are documented across 2,470 pages. Likely to stall.
alternative_effort: S if the catalogue exists, otherwise blocked indefinitely.
owner_team: QA Automation, with Product Engineering for the authoritative catalogue

issue: Several object families cannot be validated against this database at all: the AD-bridging and data-warehouse tables are entirely empty (tblLOBDetail plus about 34 others), and sso_users_accesscontrol is stale since 2026-06-11 with all four companion profile tables at 0 rows.
recommended_solution: Declare AD-bridging, data-warehouse and access-control-profile endpoints explicitly out of scope for DB validation, record why in the coverage matrix, and report their validation layer as NOT-APPLICABLE rather than FAIL.
recommended_advantages: Honest scoping - an assertion against an empty table would pass while proving nothing, which is worse than no assertion. Marking them NOT-APPLICABLE stops them inflating the failure count, the same distortion identified in DB-019. Makes the data gap visible to whoever can close it.
recommended_disadvantages: Leaves a genuine coverage hole rather than filling it, and NOT-APPLICABLE rows can be mistaken for tested rows if the report is read carelessly, so the reason string has to be carried through to the workbook.
alternative_solution: Request seeded AD-bridge and access-control data for the QA environment, and have the locked GenericScheduler ETL account unlocked so the DWH tables populate, then validate normally.
alternative_advantages: Actually closes the coverage gap instead of documenting it, and the DWH emptiness is plausibly a symptom of the locked account rather than a design choice - so unlocking it may fix a real environment fault.
alternative_disadvantages: Blocked on other teams, and unlocking GenericScheduler must be handled carefully: it is the data-warehouse ETL service account and repeated token attempts are what locked it. Seeded AD data needs an AD environment that may not exist in QA.
owner_team: QA Automation for scoping; Infrastructure / DBA for seeding and the account unlock
